newsitem.title: UK: Europe crude outlook - further gains in sight.
newsitem.headline: Europe crude outlook - further gains in sight.

text.p: European crude markets may extend recent gains this week as extra November cargoes are easily absorbed by refiners on both sides of the Atlantic racing to produce heating oil as autumn temperatures fall.
U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) inventory data published last Wednesday, which showed declines in heating oil and crude stocks, confirmed how vulnerable consumers are to a cold winter.

High North Sea freight rates, which have jumped about $7 a barrel in a week for northwest European voyages, will also help keep premiums for offshore loaders like Norwegian Statfjord at their current dizzy heights despite extra supply, traders said.

Loading programmes for the eight main North Sea export systems showed average volumes would rise by 200,000 barrels per day (bpd) to 4.6 million bpd in November, mainly due to the return of Norway's 440,000 bpd Gullfaks field.

But with European middle distillate stocks still running more than 10 percent below last year's levels, sellers are confident of finding plenty of takers for cargoes loading in the first half of November.
The Dec Brent-gas oil crack spread lost over $1 a barrel last week but stood at a healthy $6.24 a barrel on Monday.
"Margins are still relatively bouyant," said a supply manager for a European oil company.
"Refiners are running flat out and we're not seeing any meaningful (stock) builds even without the weather variable," he added.
Dated Brent would provide a solid base and should hold onto a firm premium to November paper. All four of the first November cargoes were kept early on Friday, traders said.
"Brent is looking tight in (November) 1-5 and even the first decade because of the light programme," said a North Sea producer.
November Brents were also expected to sail to the U.S. in the wake of an Ultra Large Crude Carrier, loading at the end of October, despite the apparent lack of a workable arbitrage.

The Dec Brent/WTI spread was hovering around a slim 80 cents but given the strength of Brent's closest U.S. equivalent, Louisiana Light Sweet worth 65 cents a barrel more than WTI on Friday, U.S. refiners could find the North Sea grade attractive.
"Recent U.S. buying has been slightly below their needs and European demand is buoyant - I can't see a string of cargoes waiting to hit the market," said a trader.
Med sour crudes should hold steady this week, traders said.
A planned pipeline outage at Russia's Novorossiisk is expected to keep supplies tight.
"There's hardly any Iranian around and the outage at Novo will cramp Urals," said a trader for a European major.
Maintenance work at the main pipeline supplying terminal is still planned for this week, shipping sources said on Friday.
Urals was pegged Urals at a discount of 60 cents to Dated on Friday, but one trader said he was bidding Dated -56 cents.
West African premiums should also hold current firm premiums with most Nigerian grades sold out until the third decade of November. -- Mark Thompson, London Newsroom +44 171 542 7930
